A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CREMA by the same authors, with substantial shared methods and experiments. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support a reliable comparison despite extensive revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning and zero-shot experiments on SQA3D, MUSIC-AVQA, and NExT-QA, together with fusion, modality, pre-training, and LoRA-rank analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and reports additional task evaluations, sequential-training and early-exit ablations, and training-memory measurements.

M1.justification: Equation 3 changes fusion from element-wise addition of video and gated supporting features to concatenation. Section 3.3 introduces modality-sequential updates within each minibatch and gradient-based adaptive early exit. These substantially change fusion and optimization, while retaining the frozen backbone and modality-specific adapters.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from three benchmarks to seven. v2 adds TouchQA material recognition from Touch&Go, ThermalQA past-action recognition from Thermal-IM, PerceptionTest multiple-choice QA, and VGGSound classification reformulated as QA. These extend the represented sensory domains and task requirements. Existing benchmarks and appendix-documented pre-training sources remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds Mirasol3B to the NExT-QA comparison, CMC to TouchQA/ThermalQA, and CAV-MAE plus Mirasol3B variants to VGGSound. It removes the 13B and 33B LLaMA-VQA entries from NExT-QA while retaining the 7B variant. OneLLM and X-BLIP zero-shot comparisons already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v2 evaluates expanded modality configurations, including V/P/D/N on SQA3D and V/A/F/D/N on MUSIC-AVQA. New protocols include reduced-epoch controls for adaptive stopping, a fixed-batch single-GPU memory comparison, and VGGSound accuracy both before and after excluding out-of-vocabulary predictions. These substantially extend evaluation design; retained benchmarks keep their stated evaluation splits.

E4.justification: v2 adds adaptive-exit convergence and training-budget analyses (Table 6 and Figure 2), joint-versus-sequential training ablations (Table 16), and a training-memory comparison (Table 14). Fusion and easy/hard analyses are revised. Pre-training and LoRA-rank ablations remain, and the qualitative examples are retained and regrouped rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests for its experimental results. Both primarily report point estimates; parenthesized improvements are score differences rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Many results are added or replaced. For NExT-QA, the original fused variant reports 73.0 accuracy and 1.46K GFLOPs, whereas the revised method reports 73.9 and 2.47K. New SQA3D and MUSIC-AVQA configurations report 54.6 and 81.7, respectively, under expanded modality inputs. Four added benchmarks and new training analyses supply further results. Baseline parameter counts also change, including BLIP-2 from 188M to 108M for one modality; zero-shot and rank/pre-training results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 3 revises the mathematical definition of fused queries. Sections 3.3 and 4.3 introduce a gradient-threshold stopping rule and an early-stop indicator. Existing LoRA equations remain, and neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs; the mathematical changes are limited algorithmic definitions.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate modality-sequential training and adaptive stopping into central contributions alongside fusion. Claimed empirical scope expands to seven tasks, including touch and thermal reasoning. The efficiency claim changes from approximately 96% fewer trainable parameters to over 90%, with the stated per-modality requirement changing from under 5M to 4–10M.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds substantive explanations involving incompatible modality representations, dominant-modality convergence, and the benefits of sequential optimization. It also attributes weak alternative fusion results to architectural changes and limited downstream data. Appendix C newly identifies limited temporal modeling from image-only pre-training and overhead from computing additional modalities as specific limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds dataset-construction descriptions, split sizes, and additional modality settings; Table 11 extends prompts to four new tasks, and the license section adds their sources. Most encoder, hardware, and pre-training details remain unchanged. v2 drops the explicit cross-entropy-loss statement and OneLLM reimplementation description, and does not specify a numerical early-exit threshold.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new datasets and comparators, alongside works such as VAST, ViT-Lens, and SOK-Bench. Sections 3.3 and B.4 newly acknowledge alternating adaptation and distinguish CREMA from MLA's shared classifier and gradient projection. The broader positioning against existing multimodal LLMs remains largely intact.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, integrates the separately named Espresso variant into the CREMA narrative, rewrites Section 3.3 around modular training, and reorganizes quantitative analysis around research questions. Qualitative analysis and broader impacts move into the appendix, while experimental discussions and appendix organization are substantially revised.

P2.justification: The document changes from a predominantly two-column to a single-column layout. The introductory comparison schematic is removed, the architecture diagram is redrawn with additional modalities and training information, and an early-exit plot is added. Tables are added and reorganized, while the same eight qualitative examples are regrouped into appendix figures.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for CREMA's central generality and practical-efficiency claims through touch/thermal evaluations, controlled sequential-training and early-exit analyses, and a matched-batch memory comparison (Tables 4, 6, 14, and 16). Specific temporal-modeling and preprocessing-cost limitations also improve qualification of those claims. Removed larger LLaMA-VQA comparisons, an unspecified stopping threshold, and unclear SQA3D configuration matching in Table 7 weaken parts of the presentation, but the added controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement beyond higher headline scores.
